# Introduction to the \(\SIR\) epidemic
The \(\SIR\) epidemic in a population of fixed size runs under the following stochastic dynamics:

\begin{tabbing}
Infections \qquad \= \(S\to S-1\,, I \to I+1\) occur at rate \(\alpha \, S \, I\), \kill
\emph{Infections:} \> \(S\to S-1\,, I \to I+1\) occur at rate \(\alpha \, S \, I\), \\
\emph{Removals:}   \> \(I \to I-1\,, R \to R+1\)  occur at rate \(\beta \, I\).     
\end{tabbing}

The structural parameters of epidemic duration and population size are given by 
`julia` constants,
as are the per-pair infection rate `α` and the per-individual rate of removal `β`.
```{julia}
const duration = 2.0;
const α, β = 0.2, 1.5;
const initial = SIR(0.0, 5, 1, 0);
```

```{julia}                                                                              
#| echo: false 
const MAXPOP = 20                                                                       
if initial.n > MAXPOP                                                                  
    circlabels = ["[$i]" for i in 1:initial.n]                                                                                         
else                                                                                    
    circlabels = [string(Char(codepoint('①') + i - 1)) for i in 1:initial.n]                                                           
end                                                                                     
function timelinelabels1(i) 
    if round(i) > 0 && i ≤ initial.n
        circlabels[round(Int, i)] 
    else
        "" 
    end 
end ;                                                                             
function timelinelabels2(i) 
    if i ≤ initial.n
        string(trunc(Int, i)) 
    else
        "" 
    end 
end ;                                                                             
```   

# Structure of potential infections and removals
Here is an example of a
structure recording times of potential infections (`I`),
perpetuated infections (`P`),
and of potential and conditioned removals (`R` and `C`),
using convenient abbreviations
```{julia}
A = AbstractInfection;
I = Infection;      P = PInfection;
R = Removal;        C = CRemoval;

innovation = Innovation(initial.n,
    A[  I(0.11, 2, 3), I(0.2, 2, 5), P(0.4, 1, 2), I(0.5, 2, 5),  I(0.6, 2, 4), I(0.75, 1, 2), 
        I(0.85, 3, 4), I(0.9, 2, 3), I(1.0, 2, 5), I(1.05, 4, 5), I(1.1, 2, 3), P(1.2, 2, 4), 
        I(1.45, 4, 6), I(1.5, 3, 4),  I(1.6, 3, 5)  ],
    R[  R(0.3, 5), R(0.42, 3), R(0.7, 3), R(0.55, 3), R(0.95, 5), R(1.4, 2), R(1.55, 1),
        R(1.85, 2) ],
    C[  C(1.3, 2), C(0.8, 1), C(1.7, 4), C(1.8, 4), C(1.92, 5) ])
```
Incidents are displayed using script letters corresponding to above abbreviations
(`I`/`ℐ`, `P`/`𝒫`, `R`/`ℛ`, `C`/`𝒞`).

# Constructing the epidemic
An epidemic can be constructed using a specific `initial` state
(specified as an `SIR` structure)
to commence the epidemic at time \(0.0\), and an `Innovations`
structure to hold subsequent potential infections and removals.
The epidemic simulation is
computed at the time of construction of an instance
of the `Evolution` type, defined using `initial`
together with subsequent potential incidents. 

Here is the data frame corresponding to the epidemic trajectory:
```{julia}
#| label: tbl-evolution
#| tbl-cap: Table giving evolution of the epidemic
#| echo: false 
evolution = Evolution(initial, innovation)

flow = table_trajectories1(duration, initial, evolution.trajectory)
```

# Plotting the epidemic
We now produce graphical visualizations of
the epidemic.
We condition on all activated removals being observed
(hence denoted by `C`/`𝒞`
representing "conditional removal");
we aim to derive a perfect simulation.
It is not so unrealistic to assume all activated removals are observed.

## The epidemic curve
First we draw the epidemic curve together with 
trajectories of removals and susceptibles.
Note the epidemic curve peaks at two distinct
locations, as annotated in @fig-curves.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-curves
#| fig-cap: "Epidemic curve (with annotated peaks) together with monotonic \
#|           trajectories of numbers of susceptibles and removals."
timelines = layer(flow, yintercept=1:initial.n,
    Geom.hline(style=:dot, size=0.25mm),
    style(default_color=theme.scaffold))
ll0 = layer(flow, x=:t, y=:empty, Geom.line,
    style(line_width=2theme.trail, default_color=theme.scaffold))
ll1 = layer(flow, x=:t, y=:infectives, Geom.step,
    style(line_width=theme.trail,  default_color=theme.colour(I)))
ll2 = layer(flow, x=:t, y=:removals, Geom.step,
    style(line_style=[:dashdot], line_width=theme.boundary, default_color=theme.colour(R)))
ll3 = layer(flow[flow.susceptibles.!=0, :], x=:t, y=:susceptibles, Geom.step,
    style(line_style=[:dash], line_width=theme.boundary, default_color=theme.scaffold))

fig0 = plot(timelines, 
    Coord.cartesian(xmin=0, xmax=duration, ymin=0, ymax=initial.n+0.25),
    Guide.xlabel("Process time", orientation=:horizontal),
    gadfly_theme
    )

fig1 = deepcopy(fig0)
push!(fig1, ll0, ll3, ll2, ll1,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
    text(1.2, 3.2, "Peak #1"),
    text(1.6, 3.2, "Peak #2"),
    fontsize(6pt))),
    Scale.y_continuous(labels=timelinelabels2),
    Guide.ylabel("Numbers of individuals"),
    Guide.title("Epidemic curve with removals and susceptibles")
)

depict("introduction-curves", fig1)
```

## Plotting the boundaries of zones
For the coupling construction it is convenient to suppose the
various time lines are infected in increasing index order (re-labelling symmetry
means the statistics of the
evolutions of total numbers of `susceptibles`, `infectives` and `removals` are not affected).
Thus the epidemic is now defined by boundaries between the removal zone and
the infectivity zone, and between the infectivity zone and the susceptible zone.
This is illustrated in @fig-boundary.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-boundary
#| fig-cap: "Time-evolving boundaries between susceptible, infected,     \
#|           and removed sub-populations. Note that the boundary between \
#|           susceptible and infected is itself infected; similarly the  \
#|           boundary between infected and removed is itself removed."
ll2b = layer(flow, x=:t, y=:removals, Geom.step,
    style(line_width=theme.boundary, default_color=theme.colour(R)))
ll4 = layer(flow, x=:t, y=:epidemic, Geom.step,
    style(line_width=theme.trail, default_color=theme.colour(I)))
ll5 = layer(flow, x=:t, y=:population, Geom.line,
    style(line_width=theme.trail, default_color=theme.scaffold))

fig2a = deepcopy(fig0)
push!(fig2a, ll0, ll4, ll2b, ll5,
    Scale.y_continuous(labels=timelinelabels1),
    Guide.yticks(ticks=collect(1:(initial.n))),
    Guide.ylabel("Time lines"),
)
fig2 = deepcopy(fig2a)
push!(fig2,
    Guide.title("Boundaries for the coupling construction"))

depict("introduction-boundary", fig2)
```

## Plotting infectious and removed zones
Space-time zones of infection and removal
use a blend of the original data frame with lagged data.
The actual zones of infectivity and removal (@fig-zones)
are closed at their upper boundaries: the top edge of
the infectious region is "infected", the top end of the removal region is "removed".
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-zones
#| fig-cap: "Infectivity and removal zones."
flow2 = table_trajectories2(flow, theme=theme) ;

ll6 = layer(flow2, x=:t, ymin=:removals, ymax=:epidemic, Geom.ribbon,
    alpha=[theme.opacity], style(default_color=theme.colour(I)))
ll7 = layer(flow2, x=:t, ymin=:empty, ymax=:removals, Geom.ribbon,
    alpha=[2theme.opacity], style(default_color=theme.colour(R)))

fig3a = deepcopy(fig2a)
push!(fig3a, ll6, ll7)
fig3 = deepcopy(fig3a)
fig3 = push!(fig3, 
    Guide.title("Zones of infectivity and removal"))

depict("introduction-zones", fig3)
```
```{julia}
#| label: tbl-evolution-enhanced
#| tbl-cap: Enhanced table giving evolution of the epidemic
#| echo: false
flow2
```

## Adding incidents to the plot
We now add incidents corresponding to the underlying `innovation`
using the `EpidemicsUtilities` function `draw_elements`:
see @fig-incidents.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-incidents
#| fig-cap: "Incidents arising from the `Innovation` structure,              \
#|           together with the epidemic curve and infectious and             \
#|           removal zones. Note that most of these incidents are inactive.  \
#|           The zones are closed at their upper edges: the upper boundary   \
#|           of the infectious zone is infected,            \
#|           while the upper boundary of the removal zone is removed."
fig4a = deepcopy(fig3a)
push!(fig4a,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        EpidemicsUtilities.draw_elements(innovation; theme=theme))),
    )

fig4 = deepcopy(fig4a)
push!(fig4,
    Guide.title("Incidents driving the epidemic"))

depict("introduction-incidents", fig4)
```

## Indicating activated incidents
Only some of these incidents are actually activated by the construction:

 * _Infections_ (`I`/`ℐ` and `P`/`𝒫`) must lie inside the infectivity zone and reach 
 up to the time line which at that point of time is immediately above
 the infectivity zone (and hence must reach exactly
 one time line above the highest infected time line);
 * _Removals_ (`R`/`ℛ` and `C`/`𝒞`) must lie inside the infectivity zone.

This is illustrated in @fig-activated, where the activated incidents
are emphasized by being drawn using thicker lines.
Note that perpetuated infections (`P`/`𝒫`) will arise
as part of the algorithmic time evolution of the entire \(\SIR\) trajectory.
Conditioned removals (`R`/`ℛ`)
are the _only_ removals which should be activated: if an ordinary removal
(`R`/`ℛ`) is realised then this breaks the conditioning (on all
observed removals) that we have imposed.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-activated
#| fig-cap: "Activated incidents (thicker lines) driving the epidemic:          \
#|           notice that activated removals are exactly those removals lying \
#|           in the infectivity zone, while realised infections are exactly  \
#|           those infections reaching from within the infectivity zone to   \
#|           just above it."

fig5a = deepcopy(fig4a)
push!(fig5a,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        EpidemicsUtilities.draw_activated_elements(initial, evolution.history, theme=theme)))
    )
    
fig5 = deepcopy(fig5a)
push!(fig5, 
    Guide.title("Incidents driving the epidemic, emphasizing activated incidents")
    )
    
depict("introduction-activated", fig5)
```

# Evolving the epidemic in algorithmic time
We can now give a visual explanation of how to evolve
an \(\SIR\) epidemic _in algorithmic time_,
subject to conditioning
on observed (conditioned) removals.
A single step of algorithmic time evolution can be broken down into a number of sub-steps:

1. Sample a new `Innovation` structure with fixed times for the conditional removals;
2. Remove all unconditioned removals
(those removals not activated, denoted by `R`/`ℛ`);
3. Insert precisely those removals from the new `Innovation` 
structure which will not be activated
(equivalently, which do not lie in the infectivity zone);
4. Re-sample proposed time lines for each of the conditioned removals
(denoted by `C`/`𝒞`),
accepting proposals for which the relevant conditioned removal 
is still in the infectivity zone; 
5. Now work from right to left, deciding for each old infection incident from the new `Innovation`
whether it is to be removed, and for each new infection incident from the new `Innovation`
whether it is to be introduced:
   - an old infection incident is removed unless so doing 
 would result in a conditioned removal (`C`/`𝒞`) _not_ being removed. 
 If that
 turns out to be the case, then the old infection incident is retained
 but converted into a _perpetuated_ infection (`P`/`𝒫`);
   - a new infection incident is introduced unless so doing would
 result in a potential (but not activated / conditioned) removal (`R`/`ℛ`)
 being activated.
 If that
 turns out to be the case, then the new infection incident is not introduced.
 

We will then need to address two issues. _Firstly_, we will need a convenient way of organizing 
the calculations required for making the decisions in item 5;
_Secondly_, we will need to show that the algorithmic time evolution is monotonic in some useful sense
that allows us to carry out a CFTP simulation,

## Sample a new `Innovation` structure
We first produce a new innovation `new_innovation` with conditioned removals
occurring at the same times (using `generate_innovation`) but using different time lines,
then by producing a new innovation for which the conditioned removals are obtained by altering the
time lines for the conditioned removals of the template `Innovation`.
```{julia}
innovation
```

```{julia}
new_innovation = generate_innovation(innovation, duration, α=α, β=β)
```

## Remove all inactive removals from initial `Evolution`
We now remove all unactivated removals from `innovation` to produce `iv0`, 
```{julia}
iv0 = Innovation(initial.n, innovation.infections, R[], innovation.cremovals)
```
and
plot the corresponding evolution 
```{julia}
evolution0 = Evolution(initial, iv0)
```

to obtain a modification, @fig-old-removals-gone, of @fig-activated.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-old-removals-gone
#| fig-cap: "This is @fig-activated, but with all non-activated removals taken away, \
#|           while conditioned removals are retained."

fig6a = deepcopy(fig3a)

push!(fig6a,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
    EpidemicsUtilities.draw_elements(iv0, theme=theme))),
    )

push!(fig6a,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
    EpidemicsUtilities.draw_activated_elements(initial, evolution0.history, theme=theme)))
    )
   
fig6 = deepcopy(fig6a)
push!(fig6, 
    Guide.title("The epidemic as before, deleting all non-activated removals")
    )
    
depict("introduction-old-removals-gone", fig6)
```

## Adding in inactive removals
We need to insert removals from the new innovation `new_innovation` which will not be activated by the old epidemic structure. To do this we need to extract infection and removal times for each time line, including defaults for time lines initially removed or infected, and for time lines always susceptible.
```{julia}
removal_times = sort([z.t for z in evolution0.history if typeof(z) <: AbstractRemoval])
prepend!(removal_times, repeat([0.0], initial.r))
infection_times = sort([z.t for z in evolution0.history if typeof(z) <: AbstractInfection])

# defaults for time lines initially removed or infected
prepend!(infection_times, repeat([0.0], initial.i + initial.r))
final_susceptibles = evolution0.trajectory[end].s

# defaults for time lines always susceptible
append!(infection_times, repeat([duration], final_susceptibles))
append!(removal_times, repeat([duration], final_susceptibles))

# intervals of infection for each time line
infectious_interval = collect(zip(infection_times, removal_times))
show(infectious_interval)
```

So now we must add the inactivate removals from `new_innovation`,
```{julia}
inactivated_removals = [z for z in new_innovation.removals 
        if !(infectious_interval[z.target][1] < z.t < infectious_interval[z.target][2])]
```
to the structure of innovation `iv0` to form innovation `iv1`.
```{julia}
iv1 = Innovation(initial.n, iv0.infections, inactivated_removals, iv0.cremovals)
```

Here is the resulting evolution.
```{julia}
evolution1 = Evolution(initial, iv1)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-inactive-removals
#| fig-cap: "This is @fig-old-removals-gone, but with non-activated removals added \
#|           from `new_innovation`."
fig7a = deepcopy(fig3a)

push!(fig7a,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
    EpidemicsUtilities.draw_elements(iv1, theme=theme))),
    )

push!(fig7a,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
    EpidemicsUtilities.draw_activated_elements(initial, evolution1.history, theme=theme)))
    )
   
fig7 = deepcopy(fig7a)
    
depict("introduction-inactive-removals", fig7)
```

## Re-sampling using proposed time lines for conditioned removals
Now consider the conditioned removals. For each old conditioned removal, 
```{julia}
show(innovation.cremovals)
```
see whether it can be replaced by the corresponding new conditioned removal
```{julia}
show(new_innovation.cremovals)
```
which is to say, the new conditioned removal must still be activated in
the simulation and therefore must lie in the infectious zone given by the corresponding
interval from
```{julia}
show(infectious_interval)
```

Compute
```{julia}
t0 = [tt[1] for tt in infectious_interval]
t1 = [tt[2] for tt in infectious_interval]

function accept_reject(oldcr, propcr; t0=t0, t1=t1)
    t, k = propcr.t, propcr.target
    return t0[k] ≤ t ≤ t1[k] ? propcr : oldcr
end

resultingcr = [accept_reject(oldcr, propcr) 
    for (oldcr, propcr) in zip(innovation.cremovals, new_innovation.cremovals)]
show(resultingcr)
```

Here is the new innovation
```{julia}
iv2 = Innovation(initial.n, iv1.infections, inactivated_removals, resultingcr)
```

Here is the resulting evolution.
```{julia}
evolution2 = Evolution(initial, iv2)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-processed-cremovals
#| fig-cap: "This is @fig-inactive-removals, but with accept/reject applied \
#|           to `cremovals`. Under the current seed (`2`) only the first    \
#|           conditioned removal has changed its mark."
fig8a = deepcopy(fig3a)

push!(fig8a,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
    EpidemicsUtilities.draw_elements(iv2, theme=theme))),
    )

push!(fig8a,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
    EpidemicsUtilities.draw_activated_elements(initial, evolution2.history, theme=theme)))
    )
   
fig8 = deepcopy(fig8a)
    
depict("introduction-processed-cremovals", fig8)
```
